Feature is selected, but this page shows the whole model. For a feature-only view, regenerate with the command.

One question at a time, and an answer sized to be read. Each panel states what it is for, how big the drawing is against the 12-node / 16-edge legibility budget measured for this panel, and what fell just outside the frame. Diagrams here are drawn at full size and never shrunk to fit — where long labels make one wider than the panel, drag to pan or press Fit. The whole-model pictures are still on Diagrams, where they say their own size.

Which components carry which weaknesses, and which of those pairs are still open?

Answered as a matrix, not a diagram. Every asset against every threat is the classification layer at full scale. Drawn as a node-link graph it is a bipartite incidence matrix with the hubs that shape implies; drawn as a matrix it is the same data, one cell per pair, and it stays readable at sizes where the diagram is an error box. Pick a cell to drop into the diagram for that one component.

What is this component exposed to, what defends it, and what does it talk to?

Answered as a diagram. Two diagrams, not one. The threat plane and the flow plane answer different questions, and sharing a canvas is what turns a 20-node neighbourhood into a hairball.

Everywhere this weakness was declared — and where is it still open?

Answered as a list, not a diagram. One threat across N assets is a star with N spokes, every one of them saying the same word. The picture carries no information the list does not, and stops being readable at a dozen assets.

What crosses this trust boundary, in which direction, and what defends the crossing?

Answered as a diagram. Small by construction — a boundary has two sides — so this is the one whole-scope view that is always drawable.

Where does untrusted input reach a sink with no control anywhere along the way?

Answered as chains, not a diagram. A path is the one graph shape that stays legible at any length, so each is drawn as the chain it is. These are derived from @flows and @mitigates rather than declared by anyone, so a finding here cannot cite a line that does not exist.

I am about to edit this file — what does it carry, and what else does that reach?

Answered as a diagram. The flow plane only. A shared threat is a classification, not a coupling: two components exposed to path traversal are not related, they merely have the same kind of weakness, so a hop never transits one.

What is still open, worst first?

Answered as a list, not a diagram. A ranking is a list. There is no graph question here.

L53 entitles #mcp-agent entitled to read-threat-model
By design: guardlink mcp exists to hand a connected coding agent the threat model — that disclosure is the product, not a leak. No privilege gain either: the agent already reads the annotated source these records are parsed from, so the assembled model tells it nothing it could not derive itself. AI credit is DECLARED by commit trailers, never detected from code: a commit with no trailer stays human. Pass `file` to narrow to one file. Entries carry the ledger claim key, so they join to .guardlink/verified.json. Outside a git checkout every entry is status no-git; uncommitted means the line has changes git has not seen; shallow means every introduction is a lower bound.',

L502 comment Writes `against <threat>` as well as `on <asset>`, because the join is the triple (design §9.3): a claim missing either clause matches no finding and demotes nothing. Omitting the threat here made acceptance produce a DEAD annotation — the proposal ledger carried it, the written line did not, so the only sanctioned way to create an entitlement produced one that could never work. Observed on a real repository before this fix, not hypothesised.

Entitlements1

Capabilities a principal is claimed to hold by design. The join is (actor, asset, threat) — a row with either missing joins no finding and cannot demote one. An entitlement never suppresses a finding and never gates testing; it only changes what downstream triage recommends. A claim that cites no authorization code is inert and has no effect.

Rationale
#mcp-agent read-threat-model #mcp #data-exposure src/mcp/index.ts:23
By design: guardlink mcp exists to hand a connected coding agent the threat model — that disclosure is the product, not a leak. No privilege gain either: the agent already reads the annotated source these records are parsed from, so the assembled model tells it nothing it could not derive itself. Authorization is the channel: the server is stdio-only with no network listener, so the only client is the process the operator launched, at src/mcp/index.ts:23

annotation-hash.ts:32src/parser

annotation-hash.ts:33src/parser

claim-key.ts:20src/parser

Recorded and withdrawn in .guardlink/entitlement-proposals.json — an entitlement on a covered pair is decoration
clear.ts:12src/parser
#mcp-agent is granted nothing. It can only preview a clear (dry_run defaults to true at src/mcp/server.ts:505), and a preview writes nothing, so it answers no exposure — an entitlement that joins no finding is decoration. Nor is it entitled to clear-annotations: no code makes an MCP caller obtain the confirmation its tool description asks for, so granting it would be the over-grant §2 forbids
clear.ts:13src/parser

coverage.ts:82src/parser

Pure filtering utility; no I/O
feature-filter.ts:15src/parser

feature-filter.ts:100src/parser
Metadata only: path, size, mtime. File contents are never read.

parse-file.ts:12src/parser
Regex patterns designed with bounded quantifiers and explicit structure
parse-line.ts:7src/parser

@entitles takes optional `on <asset>` and `against <threat>` clauses because the join is the (actor, asset, threat) triple, not the capability — a capability-keyed join would demote every threat on the asset including one discovered later (actor-entitlement design §9.3)
parse-line.ts:9src/parser
Scans standalone .gal files in addition to comment-based source annotations

parse-project.ts:13src/parser
Symbol matching is deliberately loose: it looks for the name as a whole word, not for a specific declaration syntax, so it works across languages
reanchor.ts:22src/parser

validate.ts:9src/parser

Writes `against <threat>` as well as `on <asset>`, because the join is the triple (design §9.3): a claim missing either clause matches no finding and demotes nothing. Omitting the threat here made acceptance produce a DEAD annotation — the proposal ledger carried it, the written line did not, so the only sanctioned way to create an entitlement produced one that could never work. Observed on a real repository before this fix, not hypothesised.
